oggetti/lune-mercurio-venere/cosa: The two planets closest to the Sun have no moons.
oggetti/lune-mercurio-venere/introduzion: Mercury and Venus are too close to the Sun: its gravity would make a moon's orbit unstable, and sooner or later the moon would crash into the planet or be torn away. That is why neither of them has any satellites.
oggetti/lune-mercurio-venere/curiosita: In the 17th and 18th centuries several astronomers believed they had seen a moon of Venus, and it was even given a name, Neith. They were really reflections inside their instruments or background stars: the moon never existed.
oggetti/lune-terra/cosa: Just one moon, but a huge one compared with the planet: a quarter of the Earth's diameter.
oggetti/lune-terra/introduzione: The Earth has only one natural satellite, the Moon. It is the fifth-largest moon in the Solar System and, compared with its planet, the largest of them all. The most widely accepted theory says it formed about 4.5 billion years ago from the debris of a huge collision between the young Earth and a body the size of Mars.
oggetti/lune-terra/curiosita: Every now and then small asteroids are captured near the Earth for a few months (the so-called "mini-moons"), but they don't stay: they are not real moons.
oggetti/lune-terra/principali/0/testo: It goes round the Earth in about 27 days and always shows us the same face. It is the only celestial body humans have ever walked on (Apollo, 1969-1972).
oggetti/lune-terra/principali/0/origine: From the Latin "luna", from the same root as "lux", light: "the shining one". The Greeks called it Selene.
oggetti/lune-marte/cosa: Two small potato-shaped moons: Phobos and Deimos.
oggetti/lune-marte/introduzione: Mars has two tiny, irregular moons, discovered in August 1877 by the American astronomer Asaph Hall at the Naval Observatory in Washington. They may be captured asteroids, or fragments from an ancient impact on Mars.
oggetti/lune-marte/curiosita: In 1726, 150 years before they were discovered, Jonathan Swift wrote in "Gulliver's Travels" that Mars had two moons. It was just a lucky invention.
oggetti/lune-marte/principali/0/testo: It orbits so close to Mars that it goes round more than three times in a Martian day. It is slowly drawing closer to the planet: in a few tens of millions of years it will crumble into a ring or crash onto Mars.
oggetti/lune-marte/principali/0/origine: Greek for "fear": he was one of the sons of Ares (Mars), who went with his father into battle.
oggetti/lune-marte/principali/1/testo: Smaller and further out. Seen from Mars it would look like little more than a bright star.
oggetti/lune-marte/principali/1/origine: Greek for "terror": the other son of Ares, brother of Phobos.
oggetti/lune-giove/cosa: 115 known moons. The four big ones, discovered by Galileo, can be seen even with binoculars.
oggetti/lune-giove/introduzione: Jupiter has 115 known moons (April 2026). Four of them are as big as planets: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, the "Galilean moons". Close to the planet there are four small inner moons; all the others are distant, tiny moons, often just a few kilometres across, which are probably captured asteroids. Many of them orbit backwards compared with Jupiter's rotation.
oggetti/lune-giove/osservare: With binoculars held very steady you can see up to four little dots in a line beside Jupiter: these are the Galilean moons. Night after night they change position.
oggetti/lune-giove/curiosita: Almost all of Jupiter's moons are named after lovers, daughters or descendants of Zeus (Jupiter), following a rule of the International Astronomical Union. The ones that orbit backwards have names ending in "e".
oggetti/lune-giove/altre: The other 58 moons of Jupiter only have a provisional code (for example S/2017 J 1): they are rocks a few kilometres across, many of them discovered from 2017 onwards.
oggetti/lune-giove/principali/0/testo: The most volcanically active body in the Solar System: hundreds of volcanoes, some with plumes hundreds of kilometres high. It is heated by the friction of the tides raised by Jupiter.
oggetti/lune-giove/principali/0/origine: In myth, Io was a priestess loved by Zeus, who turned her into a heifer to hide her from the jealous Hera. The name was proposed by Simon Marius, who claimed to have seen the moons at the same time as Galileo.
oggetti/lune-giove/principali/1/testo: Covered by a crust of ice with an ocean of salty water underneath: one of the most promising places to look for life beyond the Earth. NASA's Europa Clipper probe will reach it in 2030.
oggetti/lune-giove/principali/1/origine: The Phoenician princess carried off by Zeus, who had turned himself into a white bull. Our continent is named after her too.
oggetti/lune-giove/principali/2/testo: The largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than the planet Mercury. It is the only moon with its own magnetic field. The European probe JUICE will reach Jupiter in 2031 and then go into orbit around Ganymede.
oggetti/lune-giove/principali/2/origine: The young Trojan carried up to Olympus by Zeus, in the form of an eagle, to be cupbearer to the gods.
oggetti/lune-giove/principali/3/testo: The most heavily cratered surface in the Solar System: it has stayed almost unchanged for billions of years.
oggetti/lune-giove/principali/3/origine: The nymph loved by Zeus and turned into a bear: she is the same Callisto as in the myth of the Great Bear.
oggetti/lune-giove/principali/4/testo: The largest of the inner moons, reddish and elongated. It was the last moon discovered by eye, looking through a telescope, before the age of photography.
oggetti/lune-giove/principali/4/origine: The goat (or the nymph) who nursed the baby Zeus on the island of Crete.
oggetti/lune-giove/principali/5/testo: The largest of the distant, irregular moons. It gives its name to a family of moons that may be the pieces of a single captured asteroid.
oggetti/lune-giove/principali/5/origine: A nymph from Rhodes who bore Zeus three sons.
oggetti/lune-saturno/cosa: 293 known moons: the planet with the most moons. Titan, the largest, can be seen with a small telescope.
oggetti/lune-saturno/introduzione: Saturn has 293 known moons (June 2026), more than all the other planets put together. There is one giant moon (Titan), six medium-sized icy moons, lots of moonlets living in and near the rings, and more than 250 distant, very small moons, nearly all discovered in the last few years with large telescopes.
oggetti/lune-saturno/osservare: With a small telescope Titan looks like a tiny star beside the planet. With a medium telescope you can also see Rhea, Tethys, Dione and Iapetus.
oggetti/lune-saturno/curiosita: The distant moons are split into three families and take their names from the myths of three peoples: Inuit, Gallic and Norse (Viking) giants. The main moons, on the other hand, are named after Titans and giants of Greek mythology, brothers of Cronus, that is, Saturn.
oggetti/lune-saturno/altre: More than 220 of Saturn's moons only have a provisional code (for example S/2004 S 7). Almost all of them were announced from 2019 onwards: 128 in one go in March 2025.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/0/testo: The second-largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than Mercury. It is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, made mostly of nitrogen, and with lakes and seas, not of water but of liquid methane. In 2005 the European probe Huygens landed on it.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/0/origin: The Titans were the race of giants that Cronus (Saturn) belonged to. The name was proposed in 1847 by John Herschel, son of the man who discovered Uranus.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/1/testo: A brilliant white ball of ice that sprays jets of water into space from its south pole: there is an ocean beneath the crust. The Cassini probe flew right through them.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/1/origin: A giant of Greek mythology who fought against the gods and was buried under Sicily by the goddess Athena: his movements were the earthquakes and his breath was Etna.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/2/testo: It has an enormous crater, called Herschel, a third as wide as the moon itself: that is why it looks like the "Death Star" from Star Wars.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/2/origin: A giant of Greek mythology, killed in the war against the gods.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/3/testo: Made almost entirely of water ice. It has a huge valley, Ithaca Chasma, about 2,000 km long.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/3/origin: The Titaness Tethys, goddess of the sea, sister and wife of Oceanus.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/4/testo: Ice and rock, with long bright ice cliffs on the side that trails behind as it orbits.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/4/origin: A Titaness, in some myths the mother of Aphrodite.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/5/testo: Saturn's second-largest moon, a ball of ice covered in craters.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/5/origin: The Titaness who was the wife of Cronus and mother of Zeus.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/6/testo: It has two very different faces: one as black as coal and one as white as snow. Cassini noticed that it could only be seen on one side of its orbit and worked out why.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/6/origin: The Titan who was the father of Prometheus and Atlas.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/7/scoper: 1848, William Bond, George Bond and William Lassell
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/7/testo: An irregular moon, as porous as a sponge, that tumbles chaotically: there is no way to predict which way it will be facing.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/7/origin: The Titan who was the father of the Sun (Helios), the Moon (Selene) and the Dawn (Eos).
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/8/testo: The largest of the distant moons; it orbits backwards. It was the first moon discovered by photography.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/8/origin: The Titaness Phoebe, grandmother of Apollo and Artemis.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/9/testo: Two moons that share almost the same orbit: every four years they draw close and swap places, without ever colliding.
oggetti/lune-saturno/principali/9/origin: Janus is the two-faced Roman god of doors and passageways; Epimetheus is the brother of Prometheus.
oggetti/lune-urano/cosa: 29 moons, almost all named after characters from Shakespeare.
oggetti/lune-urano/introduzione: Uranus has 29 known moons: 14 small inner moons close to the rings, 5 large moons and 10 distant, irregular moons. Almost all were discovered by the Voyager 2 probe in 1986, by the Hubble Space Telescope and by ground-based telescopes; the latest, in 2025, by the James Webb Space Telescope.
oggetti/lune-urano/osservare: The moons of Uranus are too faint for binoculars: you need a large telescope and a very dark sky, and even then you can only see Titania and Oberon.
oggetti/lune-urano/curiosita: They are the only moons not named after myths: they are named after characters from the plays of William Shakespeare (Titania and Oberon from "A Midsummer Night's Dream", Miranda from "The Tempest") and from Alexander Pope's poem "The Rape of the Lock" (Ariel, Umbriel, Belinda).
oggetti/lune-urano/principali/0/testo: The largest moon of Uranus, with long cracks in its icy crust.
oggetti/lune-urano/principali/0/origine: The queen of the fairies in Shakespeare's "A Midsummer Night's Dream".
oggetti/lune-urano/principali/1/testo: The most distant of the large moons, dark and covered in craters.
oggetti/lune-urano/principali/1/origine: The king of the fairies, Titania's husband, in the same play.
oggetti/lune-urano/principali/2/testo: The darkest of the large moons, with a curious bright ring on one crater.
oggetti/lune-urano/principali/2/origine: A gloomy spirit in Pope's poem "The Rape of the Lock": the name recalls shadow (Latin "umbra").
oggetti/lune-urano/principali/3/testo: The brightest, with valleys and canyons that suggest a young surface.
oggetti/lune-urano/principali/3/origine: The spirit of the air in Shakespeare's "The Tempest" (and also a sylph in Pope's poem).
oggetti/lune-urano/principali/4/testo: A "patchwork" moon: patches of surface that are wildly different from one another, and a cliff, Verona Rupes, perhaps 20 km high, one of the tallest in the Solar System.
oggetti/lune-urano/principali/4/origine: The daughter of the magician Prospero in Shakespeare's "The Tempest".
oggetti/lune-nettuno/cosa: 16 moons. The big one, Triton, orbits backwards: it may be a captured dwarf planet.
oggetti/lune-nettuno/introduzione: Neptune has 16 known moons. Seven small inner moons orbit close to the rings; then comes Triton, which is huge; further out are Nereid and six other small, irregular moons.
oggetti/lune-nettuno/osservare: Triton, at about magnitude 13.5, can be seen with a 20-25 cm telescope under a dark sky. The others need professional instruments.
oggetti/lune-nettuno/curiosita: Neptune's moons are named after sea gods and Nereids, the sea nymphs who were daughters of Nereus: Neptune was the Roman god of the sea.
oggetti/lune-nettuno/principali/0/scoper: 1846, William Lassell, 17 days after Neptune was discovered
oggetti/lune-nettuno/principali/0/testo: The only large moon that orbits backwards compared with its planet: it is probably a Kuiper Belt object captured by Neptune. In 1989 Voyager 2 saw nitrogen geysers on it. It is one of the coldest surfaces ever measured, about -235 °C.
oggetti/lune-nettuno/principali/0/origin: Triton, son of Poseidon (Neptune), a fish-tailed sea god who blew into a conch shell.
oggetti/lune-nettuno/principali/1/testo: It has the most stretched-out orbit of any known moon: its distance from Neptune changes by a factor of about seven.
oggetti/lune-nettuno/principali/1/origin: The Nereids, the fifty sea nymphs who were daughters of Nereus.
oggetti/lune-nettuno/principali/2/testo: Dark and almost box-shaped: it is roughly as big as a body can be before gravity pulls it into a round shape.
oggetti/lune-nettuno/principali/2/origin: Proteus, a sea god who could change his shape at will.
oggetti/lune-plutone/cosa: Pluto has not been a planet since 2006, but it has five moons. Charon is almost half its size.
oggetti/lune-plutone/introduzione: Since 2006 Pluto has been classed as a "dwarf planet". It has five moons: big Charon and four small moons. NASA's New Horizons probe photographed them close up in July 2015.
oggetti/lune-plutone/curiosita: All the names come from the world of the dead in Greek mythology, the kingdom of Pluto (Hades).
oggetti/lune-plutone/principali/0/testo: It is so big compared with Pluto that the two of them orbit around a point in the space between them: they are almost a "double planet". They always show each other the same face.
oggetti/lune-plutone/principali/0/origin: The ferryman who carried the souls of the dead across the river Acheron.
oggetti/lune-plutone/foto/0/1: Pluto (in front) and Charon, in enhanced colours to show the differences in their surfaces. The distances are not to scale.
oggetti/lune-plutone/foto/1/1: Charon in its true colours. At the top is the reddish patch at its north pole, nicknamed Mordor.
oggetti/lune-plutone/foto/2/1: Pluto, Charon, Nix and Hydra, as New Horizons saw them. The sizes are not to scale: Nix and Hydra are about 50 km across.
oggetti/lune-esopianeti/nome: Moons of planets around other stars
oggetti/lune-esopianeti/cosa: We know of more than 6,000 planets around other stars, but not one of their moons has been confirmed yet.
oggetti/lune-esopianeti/introduzione: Exoplanets are planets that orbit other stars: more than 6,000 have been confirmed. Many are giants like Jupiter and almost certainly have moons. But a moon is small and incredibly far away, and its signal gets lost in the "noise" of the measurements: so far no moon of an exoplanet (an exomoon) has been confirmed. There are, however, a few candidates.
oggetti/lune-esopianeti/curiosita: To look for an exomoon, astronomers mainly watch a planet as it passes in front of its star: a moon can add an extra small dip in the light, or make the planet arrive a little earlier or later than expected.
oggetti/lune-esopianeti/principali/0/tes: The first major candidate: a signal seen with the Kepler and Hubble space telescopes around a giant planet about 8,000 light years away, in the constellation of Cygnus. Other research teams re-analysed the data without finding the moon: it remains unconfirmed.
oggetti/lune-esopianeti/principali/0/ori: The code means: first moon (I) of planet b of star number 1625 discovered by the Kepler telescope.
oggetti/lune-esopianeti/principali/1/tes: A second candidate around a gas giant, about 5,500 light years away, again in the area of Cygnus and Lyra. This signal has also been called into question: new observations will be needed.
oggetti/lune-esopianeti/principali/1/ori: A Kepler catalogue code: moon "i" of planet b.
oggetti/lune-esopianeti/principali/2/tes: There are other possible signals: moons of "rogue" planets found by gravitational microlensing, traces of sodium around the planets WASP-49b and WASP-12b that could come from a volcanic moon like Io, and in 2026 a possible companion of planetary mass around the brown dwarf CD-35 2722B. None of these is a confirmed exomoon.
